task.goal: Distribute urgent shared-kitchen cleanup fairly among four rotating volunteers.
hard_constraints: Volunteers overlap only 15 minutes at shift change and use a paper board.
Food-safety spills need immediate action, but no one may be assigned indefinite standby.
Measure response time, repeated burden and missed tasks over three weeks.
task.available_resources: Shift roster and existing incident notes.
task.expected_result: A fair handoff and escalation rule.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Bounded duty rotation with explicit acceptance
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a fixed rotation to determine who handles urgent cleanup during each staffed shift. On the paper board, write a primary and backup from the volunteers actually present, with start and end times taken from the roster. Rotate primary duty among the four in proportion to their staffed hours. Duty ends at the printed time; nobody owes off-shift availability.

Anyone discovering a food-safety spill immediately protects people and food using existing safe procedures and alerts the primary. If the primary cannot safely leave another task, the backup takes over. If neither can respond, stop use of the affected area and escalate to the kitchen’s existing responsible person. This requires an identified escalation recipient; the roster and incident notes alone may not establish one. Volunteers should not attempt cleanup beyond their training.

During the 15-minute overlap, outgoing and incoming volunteers inspect the board together, identify unfinished tasks, and initial each transfer. Until acceptance, the outgoing volunteer flags the area as unavailable; their shift still ends on time. An unaccepted hazardous task therefore triggers closure and escalation, not extended standby.

The mechanism makes ownership predictable while distributing scheduled responsibility. It needs only roster entries and extra columns on the board. Its limitation is that equal duty hours may still produce unequal actual cleanup work, especially when incidents cluster on particular shifts.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For three weeks, record discovery time, first protective-action time, cleanup-start time, completion or unresolved status, assigned volunteer, and cleanup minutes. Weekly, compare each person’s duty hours, incident count, cleanup minutes, consecutive assignments, and missed tasks. Use sufficiently detailed existing notes as a descriptive comparator; otherwise use an explicitly marked short baseline of current practice, retaining immediate safety action throughout. Inspect the first several handoffs for missing acceptance. Reject or revise the rule if unowned tasks recur, response becomes slower, or comparable staffed hours repeatedly produce concentrated cleanup burden. Sparse incidents cannot establish fairness reliably.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Least-burden assignment with immediate discoverer protection
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Separate immediate protection from allocation of the full cleanup. Whoever discovers a food-safety spill immediately follows existing protective procedures and alerts the other volunteers present. Among people currently available and qualified, assign the remaining cleanup to the person with the lowest accumulated cleanup minutes relative to staffed hours. Break ties with a rotating order written on the paper board. If only one eligible volunteer is present, that person acts; their work counts toward later balancing.

Keep a simple ledger beside the roster: staffed hours, cleanup minutes, incident count, and last assignment for each volunteer. Count initial containment time too, so frequent discoverers receive credit. Update after each incident, using approximate minutes consistently rather than elaborate scoring. Review the ledger during the 15-minute overlap and name an accepting owner for every unfinished task. A volunteer’s obligation ends with their scheduled shift; no assignment extends into off-shift standby.

If nobody available can safely perform the work, isolate the affected area, suspend its use, and contact the kitchen’s existing responsible person. This approach assumes that such a recipient and safe isolation procedures exist; those must be identified before use.

The mechanism directs discretionary work toward volunteers who have carried less burden, rather than merely equalizing turns. It needs paper arithmetic and honest time estimates. Availability constrains fairness: if one volunteer consistently works alone during spills, the ledger cannot redistribute that immediate work. It can only prioritize others when future choices exist.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Track every incident for three weeks: discovery, first protective action, cleanup start, completion, available volunteers, selected owner, minutes by person, and unresolved tasks at handoff. Compare response times and missed tasks with usable existing notes, acknowledging missing timestamps. For each incident with multiple eligible volunteers, also mark who a simple rotating-turn rule would have selected; this checks assignment differences, not hypothetical response times. Inspect burden per staffed hour and repeated assignments weekly. The mechanism fails its practical check if ledger consultation delays protective action, eligible lower-burden volunteers are repeatedly bypassed without recorded reasons, or unfinished tasks lose ownership. If incidents offer almost no choice of worker, report that the fairness mechanism remains largely untested.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Urgent cleanup earns an equal-time task exchange
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make urgent cleanup an exchange for scheduled routine work. Whoever discovers a food-safety spill immediately takes the protective action allowed by existing procedures. Available, qualified volunteers then complete the urgent cleanup without waiting for a fairness calculation. Every minute spent protecting the area or cleaning earns one minute of relief from transferable routine kitchen work. The mechanism compensates unavoidable interruptions by moving other work to colleagues; it can work even when the roster leaves no choice of immediate responder.

On the paper board, keep four balances and list actual routine tasks available for exchange. During each 15-minute shift overlap, match earned relief to a named task that another volunteer explicitly accepts within their scheduled hours. Record estimated minutes, then reconcile with actual time. Transfer work toward volunteers who have received more relief than they have provided. No one extends a shift, waits off duty, or receives an open-ended obligation. Unredeemed balances remain visible, with their age.

Every unfinished cleanup needs an incoming owner’s initials before the outgoing shift ends. If safe coverage is unavailable, suspend use of the affected area and escalate to an identified kitchen decision-maker; do not extend the outgoing volunteer’s duty. Establish that recipient and safe isolation procedure before starting.

This needs only the roster, board and incident notes, but assumes enough routine work is transferable and volunteers can safely perform it. It equalizes total work more directly than exposure to spills. Repeated unpleasant incidents can remain unfair despite equal minutes, so persistent concentration requires a roster change rather than declaring the balance settled.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot for three weeks. Record discovery, first protective action, cleanup start, completion, minutes by volunteer, missed tasks, accepted exchanges and balance age. Compare response times and missed tasks with usable existing notes; missing timestamps limit conclusions. Each week compare urgent minutes, consecutive incidents and total cleanup-plus-exchanged-task minutes per staffed hour. Use the same recorded workload without exchanges as a simple accounting comparator, not a claimed behavioral counterfactual. The smallest falsifying check is whether the first earned relief can actually be redeemed without dropping work. Revise if balances accumulate across weekly reviews, exchanges create missed tasks, or repeated urgent burden remains unacceptable despite relief.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Rebalance exposure through paired shift swaps
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Distribute urgent cleanup by changing who works the shifts where incidents repeatedly occur. Use the roster and existing incident notes to identify periods with concentrated spills. At each weekly review, propose paired swaps of equal staffed hours between a volunteer carrying repeated urgent work and one carrying less. Write agreed swaps on the paper board before they take effect, preserving coverage and the 15-minute overlap. This changes exposure to future incidents rather than choosing responders after a spill occurs.

Anyone discovering a food-safety spill immediately takes protective action within their training. Qualified volunteers present handle cleanup under existing safe procedures; nobody waits for a swap or fairness calculation. During overlap, both volunteers inspect unfinished work and the incoming volunteer initials acceptance. If safe cleanup or acceptance is unavailable, suspend use of the affected area and notify a designated kitchen decision-maker. Scheduled shifts end on time, with no off-duty standby.

Implementation requires only a four-person roster, incident ledger and board space for agreed swaps and unresolved tasks. Before starting, establish the escalation recipient and confirm that volunteers can exchange some shifts without losing necessary skills or coverage. Swaps must be mutually feasible; equal hours do not make inconvenient times equally acceptable.

The mechanism could reduce persistent burden when incident frequency depends on time of day and volunteers have scheduling flexibility. It cannot guarantee fairness when spills are unpredictable or availability prevents exchanges. If historical notes lack timing or worker information, the first week supplies provisional evidence rather than a confident ranking.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Over three weeks, record discovery-to-protective-action and discovery-to-cleanup-start times, completion or missed status, worker, cleanup minutes and repeated assignments. Review weekly and trial the smallest feasible paired swap after week one. Compare burden per staffed hour and consecutive assignments before and after the swap, alongside response times and missed tasks. As a simple comparator, map observed incident times onto the original roster to inspect whose exposure would have differed; this is an exposure calculation, not a prediction of behavior. The mechanism fails an initial feasibility check if no acceptable swap exists. Revise if burden simply concentrates on the replacement volunteer or coverage worsens. Few incidents leave effectiveness uncertain.

EXPAND.title: Immediate responder with compensating task exchanges
EXPAND.proposal:
Make urgent cleanup an exchange for ordinary kitchen work. Whoever discovers a food-safety spill immediately protects people and food and performs cleanup within their competence. Record their cleanup minutes on the paper board. At the next 15-minute overlap, transfer approximately equivalent, already scheduled nonurgent work from that responder to another volunteer. Spread these replacement tasks among the other three using a repeating order, skipping anyone without sufficient scheduled time. Receiving volunteers explicitly accept each exchange; nobody works beyond their shift.

This changes the fairness mechanism: urgent incidents need no allocation discussion, while their workload replaces other work instead of accumulating on frequent responders. Unlike least-burden assignment, it can compensate someone whose solo shift leaves no choice of urgent responder. Compensation is limited to actual transferable duties; an unfulfilled exchange stays visibly outstanding and must not be counted as relief delivered.

Before starting, the four volunteers use the roster and incident notes to identify transferable duties, rough durations, safe spill procedures, and an existing responsible person for escalation. These are prerequisites, not resources established by the supplied information. Do not exchange safety-critical checks or create overdue routine tasks. If safe cleanup is unavailable, immediately isolate the affected area, suspend its use, and escalate. During overlap, explicitly accept unfinished cleanup or leave the area closed with escalation recorded. All obligations end at scheduled shift boundaries.

The board needs incident timestamps, cleanup minutes, promised exchanges, acceptance and completion. Approximate duration estimates and differences in task unpleasantness limit how closely exchanges represent equal burden.
EXPAND.experiment: Run for three weeks, with one volunteer serving as record reviewer only during scheduled overlaps. Record protective-action and cleanup-start delays, repeated urgent assignments, completed compensation, and missed urgent and routine tasks. Compare total cleanup plus ordinary-duty minutes per staffed hour with the same roster under the prior bounded-duty rule, using documented exchanges to calculate the workload difference; this does not establish hypothetical response times. Use existing incident notes for response comparisons only where timestamps support them. Review weekly. Stop new exchanges if they cause a safety-critical omission or cannot fit within scheduled time; retain immediate response and escalation. Reject the mechanism if relief remains mostly promised, workload concentration persists, or routine misses increase enough to cancel its fairness benefit.

EXPAND.title: Shared response through simultaneous task division
EXPAND.proposal:
Treat an urgent spill as a short shared job for all eligible volunteers currently present, rather than assigning the whole incident to one person. Before the trial, write a simple task template on the paper board: protect people and food, obtain existing cleanup supplies, clean, and verify that reopening is safe. Use only tasks and procedures the volunteers are already qualified to perform.

The discoverer immediately begins protection and alerts those present. Available volunteers take separate necessary tasks, initialing them when practical; recording must never delay action. Divide physical cleanup into safe separate portions when possible. Nobody joins if leaving another task would create a greater immediate hazard. With only one eligible person present, that person responds alone. Do not summon off-shift volunteers.

This changes the unit of allocation from a whole incident to its component work. It could reduce repeated whole-job burdens and shorten cleanup through parallel action, particularly during the 15-minute overlap. Unlike bounded primary duty or least-burden selection, it does not choose one winner of an assignment. Its limits are substantial: narrow spaces, indivisible tasks and mostly solo shifts may leave little useful work to share, and interrupting several people may cost more total time.

At shift change, outgoing and incoming volunteers inspect each unfinished board item and explicitly transfer it to an incoming volunteer. Outgoing participation ends at the scheduled time. If no qualified person can accept, keep the affected area unavailable and contact an identified existing responsible person. Safe isolation procedures and that escalation recipient must be confirmed before starting. No new equipment or extra overlap is assumed.
EXPAND.experiment: Trial for three weeks; one volunteer checks records during scheduled overlaps. For each incident, record discovery, first protection, cleanup start, safe reopening, participants, minutes per person, interrupted duties and missed tasks. Count consecutive incidents involving each volunteer and compare burden per staffed hour. Use existing notes to compare similar incidents handled by a single responder where detail permits; otherwise report the comparison as uncertain. Inspect the first three incidents with multiple eligible volunteers: did separate tasks actually proceed simultaneously, and did reopening improve enough to justify extra person-minutes? Stop shared participation for incident types where crowding or interruptions create a safety problem, reverting to one qualified responder with isolation and escalation as needed. Reject the mechanism if repeated burdens remain concentrated or additional interruptions outweigh any response and completion benefit. Few multi-person incidents would leave the mechanism untested.

EXPAND.title: Bounded duty rotation with interruption recovery
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the bounded-duty rotation, retaining its simple assignment mechanism. On the paper board, name a primary and backup for each staffed period, using the roster to rotate duty in proportion to staffed hours. Print both duty end times. No duty extends off shift.

The changed action is a recovery rule for an interrupted cleanup: the current owner must leave the affected area safely isolated and mark the task OPEN before leaving it. Ownership transfers only when another present, qualified volunteer explicitly accepts. During the 15-minute overlap, the outgoing owner and incoming volunteer inspect unfinished items first. If their discussion is interrupted, the last accepted owner remains responsible only until their printed end time; the area stays closed after that unless an incoming volunteer accepts. A signature never substitutes for checking the actual condition.

The discoverer immediately protects people and food using established procedures and alerts the primary. If the primary cannot safely interrupt their current work, the backup accepts. If neither can act, isolate the affected area and suspend its use. Contact an existing responsible person if one is identified; do not assume that the roster establishes such a person or authority to reopen. Without a qualified responder or safe isolation procedure, stop the affected activity and seek qualified assistance.

This preserves predictable coverage while closing a gap between an accepted assignment and a cleanup interrupted later. It needs only roster entries and board marks. Compared with the original rotation, it adds a short status update but may prevent tasks silently losing ownership. Equal duty hours can still produce unequal cleanup work; review actual burden rather than claiming the rotation guarantees equality.
EXPAND.experiment:
Run for three weeks. The outgoing primary checks board completeness during each existing overlap; rotate this recording duty with primary duty. Record discovery, first protective action, cleanup start, completion, each volunteer’s cleanup minutes, interruptions, accepted transfers, and tasks missed or still open at shift end. Compare response times with existing notes only where their timestamps support comparison. Review incident counts, consecutive assignments and cleanup minutes per staffed hour weekly.

Before starting, walk through three paper cases during one overlap: a primary who can safely stop their ordinary task; a primary who cannot safely interrupt, requiring backup acceptance; and an unfamiliar spill outside everyone’s competence, requiring closure and qualified assistance. Also interrupt a simulated handoff and verify that ownership and closure remain explicit without extending either shift.

Stop using the handoff procedure if it permits an unsafe reopening or creates an ownership gap; retain closure and immediate protection while correcting the rule. Repeated burden concentration triggers revision of future duty allocation among compatible staffed periods. Sparse incidents or incomplete historical timestamps limit conclusions.

EXPAND.title: Least-burden allocation with a safe stopping-point check
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade least-burden assignment by checking whether a proposed owner can reach a safe stopping point within their remaining scheduled time. The original rule accounts for availability but does not specify how to handle a volunteer who is available now yet about to leave.

The discoverer immediately protects people and food; allocation must not delay that action. Among present, qualified volunteers who can safely interrupt other work, choose the person with the lowest recorded cleanup minutes per staffed hour, breaking ties with a rotating order on the board. Before accepting, that person checks whether they can finish or leave the work safely isolated before their shift ends. If not, choose the next eligible person. Uncertain duration is a reason to plan a safe stopping point, not to promise completion.

If nobody can finish, a qualified present volunteer performs whatever immediate containment they can safely complete within their shift. Keep the area closed and list the remaining work. An incoming volunteer accepts it during the 15-minute overlap after inspecting its condition. Before acceptance, the current owner retains responsibility only within their scheduled hours. An interrupted handoff leaves the task OPEN and the area closed; nobody inherits it merely by arriving. If safe containment is unavailable, suspend the affected activity and seek qualified assistance through an identified existing contact, if available.

Count containment, partial cleanup and handoff work in each person’s cleanup minutes. Write the reason whenever the lowest-burden person is skipped. The current responder makes the immediate selection; incoming and outgoing volunteers update the ledger during overlap. This requires paper arithmetic, approximate time estimates and known safe procedures. Compared with unrestricted least-burden selection, it may assign more work to someone with a longer remaining shift, but avoids allocating a whole task that immediately needs reassignment. Scheduling constraints may still prevent equal burdens.
EXPAND.experiment:
Trial for three weeks, with the incoming volunteer checking ledger completeness during each overlap. Record discovery, first protection, cleanup start, completion or open status, eligible volunteers, remaining shift time, selection or skip reason, and minutes contributed by each person. Weekly compare response times, repeated assignments, cleanup minutes per staffed hour and missed urgent or routine tasks. Existing notes provide a comparator only where sufficiently detailed.

First inspect three cases: a low-burden volunteer with enough time for a familiar cleanup; the same volunteer near shift end when another qualified person has sufficient time; and an unfamiliar spill whose duration or safe treatment is unknown. Verify that protection starts immediately, uncertainty leads to safe isolation, and a failed or interrupted transfer does not extend a shift.

Stop using the stopping-point estimate as an allocation filter if it delays protective action or repeatedly produces unsafe stopping conditions. Revert to immediate qualified response with closure and explicit handoff while revising the filter. If longer-shift volunteers accumulate repeated extra work, change subsequent discretionary assignments using the ledger. With few incidents offering a choice of responder, report the allocation benefit as untested.

EXPAND.title: Rotate spill-producing duties and attach cleanup to the task
EXPAND.proposal:
Use responsibility for the activity creating a spill as the primary allocation mechanism. Instead of treating every incident as detached shared work, the volunteer currently performing a clearly identifiable kitchen task also owns its safe cleanup. Rotate recurring, transferable spill-producing duties among the four during their existing staffed shifts, in proportion to staffed hours and subject to qualification. This distributes exposure to cleanup and may encourage prevention.

At the first overlap, use the roster and incident notes to identify whether any such duties actually exist. Put only those duties and their current operators on the paper board. Do not infer blame from proximity or investigate causation during an emergency. The discoverer immediately protects people and food. A clearly identified task operator then performs cleanup if present, qualified and able to interrupt safely. For an unattributed spill, absent operator or unavailable operator, use a posted bounded responder rotation among present volunteers. No one is called back or remains on standby after their shift.

During each 15-minute overlap, inspect unfinished cleanup before transferring the associated activity. Until explicit acceptance, the outgoing operator owns the task within their shift and keeps the affected area isolated. If acceptance is interrupted or absent at shift end, leave the activity suspended and the board marked OPEN. Seek qualified assistance through an existing responsible contact if one is identified. Reopening requires the kitchen’s established safe procedure; the board does not create that authority.

The distinct lever is distributing the activities that generate cleanup, rather than selecting a responder after every incident. It needs only a short duty map and the existing board. It assumes useful duties can be transferred safely within existing shifts. If the notes show mostly unrelated or unattributable spills, omit this route and use bounded responder rotation. Compared with that simpler rotation, this adds duty planning and may shift undesirable ordinary work; its prevention and fairness benefits are uncertain.
EXPAND.experiment:
Run a three-week trial only if the initial inspection identifies recurring, transferable duties linked to spills. During each overlap, the incoming volunteer checks the duty map and open tasks. Record duty exposure time, incident association or uncertainty, discovery, first protection, cleanup start, completion, cleanup minutes by person, repeated assignments and missed urgent or routine tasks.

Review weekly whether duties and cleanup burden are concentrated relative to staffed hours. Where a duty creates repeated burden for one person, rotate its next compatible occurrence to another qualified volunteer; do not transfer it to someone without capacity. Compare response and missed-task measures with usable incident notes, and compare board effort with the simpler bounded rotation. A falling spill count would be suggestive, not proof of prevention over three weeks.

Walk through a clear task-linked spill, a spill whose operator cannot safely interrupt another activity, and an unfamiliar spill with uncertain origin or treatment. The latter two must trigger immediate protection and fallback without attribution debate. Stop task-linked allocation if it delays response, prompts disputes, creates unsafe duty transfers or increases missed work; revert to bounded responder rotation. If duties cannot actually rotate, this mechanism cannot establish fair exposure and should end.
